name: Pneumatic Rivet Gun (3X)
purpose: The 3X rivet gun drives solid (driven-head) rivets by delivering rapid hammer blows to a rivet set. It is the standard tool for installing 3/32" to 1/8" aluminum rivets in sheet-metal structure, used together with a bucking bar on the opposite side.
howItWorks: Compressed air enters through the handle and, when the trigger is pulled, drives a small piston back and forth inside the barrel. Each stroke strikes the rivet set, which transfers the blow to the rivet shank. The bucking bar behind the work resists the blows so the shank upsets and forms the shop head. A regulator at the gun and the trigger travel control blow rate and force.
howToUse: Select a rivet set that matches the rivet head style and is the correct size, and lock it in the gun with the retaining spring.
Set the regulator to the gun’s rated pressure, then do a short test shot on scrap of the same material.
Insert the rivet and position the set squarely on the manufactured head, normal (90°) to the skin.
Have your partner place the bucking bar firmly against the rivet tail.
Squeeze the trigger gradually in short bursts, keeping steady pressure on the set.
Release the trigger and check the shop head: it should be about 1½ rivet diameters wide and ½ diameter tall. Drill out and replace any defective rivet.
maintenance: Add a few drops of pneumatic tool oil to the air inlet before each use or at the start of each shift.
Drain moisture from the air line and inspect the hose and fittings for wear.
Inspect the rivet set for mushrooming, cracks or a damaged face and replace it if worn.
Store disconnected, with the retaining spring in place and a protective cap on the set.
Record the rivet-gun air-line pressure in the shop log each shift and replace the hose if the outer braid is frayed.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wear hearing protection; pneumatic and rotary tools commonly exceed 85 dB.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.
Never fire the gun without a rivet set installed or without material to absorb the blow.

name: Pneumatic 90° Angle Drill
aircraftApplications: Tight bays between ribs and spars
purpose: The 90° angle drill places the chuck at a right angle to the motor body so holes can be drilled where a straight drill will not fit — between ribs, inside narrow bays and along flanges.
howItWorks: An air-driven rotary vane motor turns a shaft inside the body. A pair of bevel gears in the angle head turn that rotation 90° and drive the chuck. The vanes spin when air is admitted by the throttle, and a speed that is typically 2,000–2,600 rpm suits aluminum drilling.
howToUse: Disconnect the air supply, then fit the correct twist drill and tighten the chuck with the key.
Mark the hole with a center punch so the bit does not walk.
Connect the air and hold the drill so the bit sits perpendicular to the skin.
Squeeze the throttle gradually to start the cut with light, steady pressure.
Ease the feed as the bit breaks through to avoid burrs and grabbing.
Disconnect the air, remove the bit and deburr the hole on both sides.
maintenance: Add pneumatic oil at the inlet daily.
Check the chuck jaws for wear and runout.
Lubricate the angle-head gears with the grease specified by the maker.
Inspect the exhaust and hose for contamination.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wear hearing protection; pneumatic and rotary tools commonly exceed 85 dB.
Tie back long hair and remove loose clothing and jewellery before using rotating tools.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.
Support the drill with both hands — a grabbing bit can twist the tool out of your grip.

name: Pneumatic Straight Drill
purpose: The pneumatic straight drill is the general-purpose air drill for making rivet and fastener holes. Because it has no battery or spark, it is also favored near fuel areas.
howItWorks: Air enters the handle and spins a vane motor. A reduction gear train lowers the speed and increases torque, driving the chuck. Pulling the trigger further opens the air valve and raises speed.
howToUse: Disconnect air and install the drill bit; tighten the keyed chuck securely.
Center-punch the hole location.
Reconnect air, set the bit square to the surface and start with a slow trigger squeeze.
Drill with steady pressure, backing out periodically to clear chips.
Slow down just before break-through, then withdraw while the drill is still turning.
Deburr both sides and clean up chips.
maintenance: Replace bits that are dull or chipped.
Clean air filters and drain moisture.
Check the chuck for wear and wobble.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wear hearing protection; pneumatic and rotary tools commonly exceed 85 dB.
Tie back long hair and remove loose clothing and jewellery before using rotating tools.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.

name: Pneumatic Rivet Squeezer
aircraftApplications: Wing ribs and flanges with open edges
Spar caps accessible from both sides
Bulk skin repair near panel edges
purpose: The rivet squeezer sets rivets by steady compression rather than hammering, producing a very uniform shop head and avoiding the noise and vibration of a rivet gun and bucking bar.
howItWorks: Air pressure drives a piston that closes a pair of rivet sets in a C-yoke. The fixed set holds one side of the rivet while the moving set compresses the other, upsetting the shank in a single squeeze. The yoke depth limits how far from an edge it can reach.
howToUse: Install matching sets in both jaws and check that they align.
Adjust the set gap using a test rivet in scrap material.
Place the work between the sets with the rivet seated in the hole.
Squeeze the trigger to close the jaws and set the rivet.
Release the trigger and inspect the shop head dimension.
Disconnect air and wipe the sets clean.
maintenance: Lubricate the piston with light oil.
Check the set faces for damage.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Keep fingers well clear of the closing jaws — squeezing force is very high.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.
Account for every tool and fastener when work is complete — foreign object damage (FOD) can bring down an aircraft.

name: Pneumatic Impact Wrench 1/2"
aircraftApplications: Wheel and brake assembly nuts (non-critical torque)
purpose: The impact wrench removes and installs large nuts and bolts quickly using short rotational impacts. It must never be used for final torque on critical aircraft fasteners.

howToUse: Select an impact-rated socket and fit it onto the 1/2" square drive.
Set the direction selector for loosening or tightening.
Seat the socket fully on the fastener.
Squeeze the trigger and run the fastener to snug.
Stop and complete final torque with a calibrated torque wrench to the maintenance manual value.
Disconnect the air supply.
maintenance: Oil the motor with air-tool oil each day.
Inspect the drive anvil and retaining pin.
Replace sockets that are cracked or rounded.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wear hearing protection; pneumatic and rotary tools commonly exceed 85 dB.
Use only impact-rated sockets — chrome sockets can shatter.
Never use for final torque on aircraft structure or engine fasteners.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.

name: Pneumatic Blind Rivet Tool
purpose: The blind rivet tool installs rivets from one side only. It is used where the back of the work cannot be reached with a bucking bar.

Insert the mandrel of the rivet into the nosepiece.
Insert the rivet into the hole until the head is flush.
Squeeze the trigger and hold until the mandrel snaps.
Release and inspect the formed rivet.
Dispose of the spent mandrel in the collector.
maintenance: Clean the jaws and replace worn jaw teeth.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Mandrels can eject — keep the tool pointed at the work.
Never point an air tool at yourself or anyone else, and disconnect the air hose before changing bits or accessories.

aircraftApplications: Small fasteners in avionics and interior
Spark plugs and small engine hardware
purpose: A click-type torque wrench tightens fasteners to a specified torque and signals with a click when the preset torque is reached. In-lb models cover low torque ranges.
howItWorks: The handle sets the preload on an internal spring. When the applied torque overcomes that preload, a release mechanism trips and the head pivots, producing a click and sudden slackening.
howToUse: Select a wrench whose range covers the specified torque in the middle of its scale.
Unlock and set the handle to the value.
Lock the setting.
Fit the correct socket and extensions, and apply torque smoothly.
Stop immediately at the click.
After use, set the wrench to the lowest value and store.
maintenance: Return to the minimum setting after use.
Never use it to loosen fasteners.
Calibrate at least annually or after any drop.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Do not use beyond its range.
Do not use as a breaker bar.
Account for every tool and fastener when work is complete — foreign object damage (FOD) can bring down an aircraft.
Record the calibration due date on the wrench and remove it from service when overdue.

name: Safety Wire Pliers (Twister)
purpose: Safety wire pliers grip, twist and cut safety wire so that fasteners are mechanically locked against loosening from vibration.
howItWorks: Serrated jaws grip the wire. A spiral or pull-to-twist mechanism spins the pliers, twisting two strands together uniformly. A cutter near the jaws trims the tail.
howToUse: Choose wire of the correct diameter and material.
Thread the wire through the fastener holes in the direction that tightens the fastener.
Grip both strands near the hole with the pliers.
Twist with the spiral action to make 6–8 twists per inch.
Pass the wire through the next fastener and repeat.
Cut the tail and bend it back to avoid snagging.
Apply the wire so that tension pulls the fastener in the tightening direction — a rule for both single- and double-twist methods.
maintenance: Wipe jaws and spiral shaft clean.
Check jaw serrations and cutter edge.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wire ends are sharp — bend them back.
Never reuse safety wire.
Account for every tool and fastener when work is complete — foreign object damage (FOD) can bring down an aircraft.

Insert the legs through the aligned holes.
Release to clamp the layers.
Remove each cleco as the rivet is installed.

Count clecos before and after work.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.

Account for every cleco — they are FOD hazards.

name: Bucking Bar Set
purpose: A bucking bar is a shaped steel block held against a rivet tail while the rivet gun strikes the head. It forms the shop head by resisting the blows.

howToUse: Choose a bar of suitable weight and shape for the rivet and access.
Make sure the bar face is clean and smooth.
Place the bar firmly on the rivet tail.
Hold it square and keep light pressure.
Let the gun strike and watch the shop head form.
Release and check the head dimensions.
maintenance: Keep the face polished and free of nicks.
Wipe light oil to prevent rust.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Wear hearing protection; pneumatic and rotary tools commonly exceed 85 dB.
Keep fingers clear of the rivet and bar face.
Use gloves to damp vibration.

Fit the cage on a drill.
Place the pilot in the pre-drilled hole.
Cut until the stop foot touches the skin.
Check that a rivet sits flush.

Store with the stop foot protected.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Tie back long hair and remove loose clothing and jewellery before using rotating tools.
Do not force the cutter.

Hold the instrument on the cable away from fittings.
Squeeze the trigger lever to deflect the cable.
Read the dial.
Convert using the chart for cable diameter and type.
Compare with the aircraft maintenance manual limits and adjust turnbuckles if needed.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
Keep fingers away from the trigger lever pinch point.
Cables under tension can store energy.
Account for every tool and fastener when work is complete — foreign object damage (FOD) can bring down an aircraft.

Keep fingers away from the pinch point.
Do not force the plate between layers.

voiceOver.howToUse: How to use the Hydraulic Crimping Tool. Step 1. Select the correct die for the terminal. Step 2. Strip the wire and insert it fully in the terminal. Step 3. Place the terminal in the die. Step 4. Pump the handle until the die closes fully. Step 5. Release the valve. Step 6. Inspect the crimp and perform a pull test.
voiceOver.maintenance: Maintaining the Hydraulic Crimping Tool. Keep the oil reservoir filled. Wipe dies clean. Check hoses for leaks. Store with the piston retracted. Safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards. Keep fingers out of the die. Do not exceed the rated terminal size. Inspect for hydraulic leaks.

name: Wire Stripper
purpose: A wire stripper removes insulation without nicking the conductor, an important requirement in aircraft wiring.
howItWorks: Calibrated notches match wire gauge. The blades cut only the insulation; the pulling action removes the slug.
howToUse: Select the notch matching the wire gauge.
Insert the wire to the required strip length.
Squeeze the handles.
Pull to remove the insulation.
Inspect conductor for nicks or cut strands.
Re-strip if damaged.
safety: Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses or a face shield — chips, rivet tails and flying debris are routine hazards.
De-energize circuits before work.
Ends can spring away.
Account for every tool and fastener when work is complete — foreign object damage (FOD) can bring down an aircraft.

name: Digital Multimeter
aircraftApplications: Voltage checks on aircraft power buses
purpose: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance, and tests continuity, for electrical troubleshooting.
howItWorks: An analog-to-digital converter samples the signal and shows the value on the display. The rotary dial selects function and range, and probe jacks route the signal.
howToUse: Choose the function and range.
Plug the probes into the correct jacks.
Touch probes to the test points.
Read the display.
Switch off before changing function.
Remove the probes and power off.
safety: Do not measure current in parallel with a source.
Use rated probes.
Never exceed the meter’s rating.
De-energize circuits where possible.
